    Generating drift¶

    Drift is a systematic shift of the data distribution: the same data-generating process starts producing values that are translated (or scaled) compared to the values observed before.

    This notebook shows the two levers available in badgers to inject drift, in increasing complexity:

    1. Acting on the observation process — directly translate the observed values of one or several columns (this can represent a change in the measurement process, a systematic bias in a sensor, etc.). No causal model is involved; these generators do not use a DGP and do not propagate anything: the change is exactly the shift requested. badgers offers them in two flavors:
      • deterministic (FixedShiftGenerator, FixedShiftClassesGenerator): every affected value is translated by exactly the requested amount, in a fully reproducible way;
      • random (RandomShiftGenerator, RandomShiftClassesGenerator): the shift magnitude is drawn from a normal distribution whose standard deviation is the requested amount.
    2. Acting on the data-generating process (DGP) — perturb a node of a fitted causal model and let the shift propagate to the descendants through the structural equations (CausalDriftGenerator).

    All of them accept a selector to decide which rows are affected (see the Understanding badgers notebook for the selector contract).

    Goal¶

    Translate the data distribution: deterministic fixed shifts first, then random shifts with signed per-column magnitudes, then per-class drift on a causal graph.

    RandomShiftGenerator, RandomShiftClassesGenerator,
)

rng = default_rng(seed=0)

    Part A — Acting on the observation process (no DGP)¶

    What these generators do: they standardize X (each column to mean 0, variance 1), add the shift, and un-standardize. The result is a translation of the observed values only — no causal structure is used, and nothing propagates beyond the shifted columns.

    Deterministic: translate all rows (FixedShiftGenerator)¶

    Every value of the selected columns is translated by exactly shift standard deviations (the parameter may be a scalar or a signed per-column array). No random number is drawn, so the same input always produces the same output — useful for controlled, reproducible benchmark scenarios.

    In [3]:
    Copied! 
    gen = FixedShiftGenerator(random_generator=rng)
Xt = gen.generate(X=X.copy(), shift=np.array([2., -2.]))
# verify: the shift is EXACTLY `shift` sigma units per column
delta = Xt - X
assert np.allclose(delta, np.array([2., -2.]) * X.std(axis=0, ddof=0))
    gen = FixedShiftGenerator(random_generator=rng) Xt = gen.generate(X=X.copy(), shift=np.array([2., -2.])) # verify: the shift is EXACTLY `shift` sigma units per column delta = Xt - X assert np.allclose(delta, np.array([2., -2.]) * X.std(axis=0, ddof=0))

    Deterministic: translate per class (FixedShiftClassesGenerator)¶

    The class values are read from a column of X (here the last column, cls, position 2). A ClassSelector builds one boolean mask per class value: each class gets its own shift — here given as a dict {class_value: shift}. Every class value present among the selected rows must have an entry (a missing one raises ValueError); plain-int keys work for a float-encoded class column (keys are normalized against its dtype).

    Note: the class column is never shifted (it defines which rows are affected, so modifying it would corrupt the selection). The class column is read from the selector's class_column — the selector owns the class information. Pass variables= to restrict/override the columns that get shifted.

    In [5]:
    Copied! 
    from badgers.core.selectors import AlwaysSelector, ClassSelector

# columns: f0=0, f1=1, cls=2 ? selectors take int positions
selector = ClassSelector([0, 1], class_column=2,
                         proportions={0: 1., 1: 1., 2: 1., 3: 1.}, rng=rng)

gen = FixedShiftClassesGenerator(random_generator=rng)
Xt = gen.generate(X=Xc.copy(), selector=selector,
                  shift={0: 4.0, 1: 2.0, 2: 4.0, 3: 0.0})
    from badgers.core.selectors import AlwaysSelector, ClassSelector # columns: f0=0, f1=1, cls=2 ? selectors take int positions selector = ClassSelector([0, 1], class_column=2, proportions={0: 1., 1: 1., 2: 1., 3: 1.}, rng=rng) gen = FixedShiftClassesGenerator(random_generator=rng) Xt = gen.generate(X=Xc.copy(), selector=selector, shift={0: 4.0, 1: 2.0, 2: 4.0, 3: 0.0})

    Random: translate all rows (RandomShiftGenerator)¶

    Same contract as the deterministic version, but the shift actually applied is drawn from a normal distribution: for each column the draw is N(0, shift_std) * sign(shift_std) — the absolute value of shift_std sets the scale, its sign sets the direction. With a scalar shift_std all columns get independent draws of the same scale.

    In [7]:
    Copied! 
    gen = RandomShiftGenerator(random_generator=rng)
Xt = gen.generate(X=X.copy(), shift_std=np.array([2., -2.]))
    gen = RandomShiftGenerator(random_generator=rng) Xt = gen.generate(X=X.copy(), shift_std=np.array([2., -2.]))

    What shift / shift_std / shift_amount actually mean¶

    Both parameters express the shift in units of the column's standard deviation (sigma). Internally every drift generator does:

    z = (X - mean) / std          # normalize: each column has sigma = 1
z += shift                    # deterministic (FixedShift*): the parameter IS the shift
                              # random: shift ~ N(0, shift_std * sigma)
X' = z * std + mean           # un-normalize

    So shift = 2 / shift_std = 2 on column f0 means exactly: "move column f0 by 2 of its own standard deviations" — a column with a wide range gets a proportionally larger absolute shift than a narrow one. The shift is a single value per column, applied to all affected rows (that is what makes it drift and not noise — noise redraws per row). The deterministic generators apply it verbatim; the random ones draw it once.

    In [13]:
    Copied! 
    # verify the semantics: the shift DRAWN for f0, expressed in sigma units,
# equals a draw from N(0, shift_std) -- i.e. shift_std sets the scale of the
# shift in standard deviations, it is not the shift itself.
X_test = X[:, :2].astype(float).copy()
gen = RandomShiftGenerator(random_generator=default_rng(42))
Xt_test = gen.generate(X_test, shift_std=np.array([2.0, 0.0]))

sigma0 = X_test[:, 0].std()                 # sigma of the ORIGINAL column
observed_z = (Xt_test[:, 0] - X_test[:, 0]).mean() / sigma0
expected_z = default_rng(42).normal(0., 2.0, size=2)[0]  # the same draw
print(f'shift of f0 in sigma units: {observed_z:.4f}')
print(f'draw from N(0, shift_std=2):  {expected_z:.4f}')
print('match:', np.isclose(observed_z, expected_z))
print('f1 untouched:', np.allclose(Xt_test[:, 1], X_test[:, 1]))
    # verify the semantics: the shift DRAWN for f0, expressed in sigma units, # equals a draw from N(0, shift_std) -- i.e. shift_std sets the scale of the # shift in standard deviations, it is not the shift itself. X_test = X[:, :2].astype(float).copy() gen = RandomShiftGenerator(random_generator=default_rng(42)) Xt_test = gen.generate(X_test, shift_std=np.array([2.0, 0.0])) sigma0 = X_test[:, 0].std() # sigma of the ORIGINAL column observed_z = (Xt_test[:, 0] - X_test[:, 0]).mean() / sigma0 expected_z = default_rng(42).normal(0., 2.0, size=2)[0] # the same draw print(f'shift of f0 in sigma units: {observed_z:.4f}') print(f'draw from N(0, shift_std=2): {expected_z:.4f}') print('match:', np.isclose(observed_z, expected_z)) print('f1 untouched:', np.allclose(Xt_test[:, 1], X_test[:, 1]))

    Part B — Acting on the data-generating process (DGP)¶

    What the generator does: CausalDriftGenerator takes a fitted DGP (a causal model of the data). It shifts a node of choice, then re-evaluates the structural equations of the descendants on the shifted rows (Pearl surgery): the change propagates exactly as it would in the real system. Only downstream nodes are affected; upstream nodes and untouched rows stay as they were.

    In [14]:
    Copied! 
    import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import networkx as nx
import pandas as pd

import dowhy.gcm as gcm
from badgers.core.dgp.backends import GcmSCMDGP
from badgers.generators.tabular_data.drift.causal import CausalDriftGenerator


def make_scm(graph):
    scm = gcm.StructuralCausalModel(graph)
    for node in graph.nodes:
        if not list(graph.predecessors(node)):
            scm.set_causal_mechanism(node, gcm.EmpiricalDistribution())
        else:
            scm.set_causal_mechanism(node, gcm.AdditiveNoiseModel(
                prediction_model=gcm.ml.create_linear_regressor()))
    return scm

    1. Build the causal graph¶

    We use a three-node chain X -> Y -> Z. The node names are symbolic; a column_mapping maps them to column positions of X.

    In [16]:
    Copied! 
    # --- Build the chain X -> Y -> Z ---
chain = nx.DiGraph()
chain.add_edges_from([("X", "Y"), ("Y", "Z")])

draw_graph(chain, title="Chain: X → Y → Z")
plt.show()
    # --- Build the chain X -> Y -> Z --- chain = nx.DiGraph() chain.add_edges_from([("X", "Y"), ("Y", "Z")]) draw_graph(chain, title="Chain: X → Y → Z") plt.show()

    2. Generate data from the DAG¶

    Each node is a weighted sum of its parents plus noise, so the data already carries the causal structure the generator will exploit.

    3. Fit the DGP¶

    The GcmSCMDGP adapter wraps a dowhy.gcm.StructuralCausalModel: every non-root node's mechanism is a linear AdditiveNoiseModel fitted on the original data, root nodes resample the observed values. The SCM is built with dowhy-gcm's own API (see the make_scm helper).

    In [19]:
    Copied! 
    dgp = GcmSCMDGP(make_scm(chain), column_mapping).fit(X.copy())

gen = CausalDriftGenerator(random_generator=np.random.default_rng(0), dgp=dgp)
    dgp = GcmSCMDGP(make_scm(chain), column_mapping).fit(X.copy()) gen = CausalDriftGenerator(random_generator=np.random.default_rng(0), dgp=dgp)

    Propagation to the descendant (Y → Z)¶
    The drift is a single systematic shift, but the propagation is Pearl surgery with fresh noise: Z is not translated by a rigid delta — it is recomputed from its (shifted) parent through the fitted structural equation, Z_new = f(Y_shifted) + fresh_noise. The systematic part of the shift carries through (Z moves because Y moved), but Z's scatter is re-rolled, not preserved: the descendant cloud keeps roughly its original width while its position follows the parent's shift. This is what distinguishes drift from noise: drift shifts a node systematically (one draw applied to all affected rows), noise scatters it row-by-row — and in both cases the descendants' noise is freshly drawn, never inherited.

    • Drift is a single systematic shift per column, applied to all
affected rows — in contrast to noise, which redraws per row.
      • 

    • shift_std / shift_amount / shift are in units of the column's
standard deviation (normalize, shift, un-normalize).
      • 

    • The class column is never shifted by the per-class generators (it
defines the selection); it is read from the selector's
class_column — the selector owns the class information. Use
variables= (int positions) to make the shifted columns explicit.
      • 

    • Generators mutate X in place — pass X.copy() to keep the
original.
      • 

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    Takeaways¶
      

    • Drift translates columns in units of their standard deviation (data are standardized first).
      • 

    • FixedShiftGenerator is deterministic (same input, same output); RandomShiftGenerator draws one shift per column with a signed magnitude.
      • 

    • Per-class drift (RandomShiftClassesGenerator) never shifts the class column itself.
      •
